prompt: How did Ernest Vincent Wright make sure no letter E slipped into Gadsby?
options: He tied down the E type-bar of his typewriter
He had a proofreader cross out every E afterwards
He wrote the book in a code that has no E
He used a typewriter that was built without an E key
correctAnswer: He tied down the E type-bar of his typewriter
explanation: His introduction says the E type-bar was tied down with string, so the typewriter could not print the letter. He reported that the job took five and a half months of concentrated work.

prompt: Apart from its introduction, the first printing of Gadsby contains no letter E at all.
explanation: Almost, but not quite: three stray copies of "the" and the word "officer" slipped into the first print run. Wright also had the printer leave the word "Chapter" off the chapter headings because of its E.

prompt: Georges Perec's 1969 novel without the letter E, translated by Gilbert Adair as A Void, is called La __________.
explanation: The title means "The Disappearance", which is also the plot: Anton Voyl vanishes and his friends die whenever they are about to say a word with an E in it.

prompt: What rule does each chapter of Christian Bök's Eunoia obey?
options: It uses only one of the five vowels
It leaves out a different letter of the alphabet
Every sentence reads the same backwards
No word in it is longer than five letters
correctAnswer: It uses only one of the five vowels
explanation: Each chapter is a univocal lipogram: Chapter A uses only A, Chapter E only E, and so on. Bök also left out Y, and every chapter includes a banquet, a debauch and a voyage.

prompt: Match each book to its constraint:

pairs.right: Over 50,000 words in English with no E
A French novel with no E and no chapter five
An English translation that keeps the no-E rule
Five chapters, each with a single vowel

explanation: All four are lipograms, texts that deliberately leave letters out. Eunoia was directly inspired by Perec's group, the Oulipo, whose members write under self-imposed rules like these.

prompt: Where did James McAuley and Harold Stewart get the words for Ern Malley's poems?
options: From the books in front of them, including a manual on mosquito control
From lines translated out of forgotten French poets
From letters sent home by soldiers at the front
From words picked by rolling dice against a dictionary
correctAnswer: From the books in front of them, including a manual on mosquito control
explanation: They wrote the lot in one afternoon at the Victoria Barracks in Melbourne, then typed the poems on army typewriters. Their stated aim was to see whether an editor could tell nonsense from real poetry.

prompt: PublishAmerica accepted Atlanta Nights, the deliberately terrible novel written to test it.
explanation: It did. The authors revealed the hoax before signing, because the contract would have guaranteed a single real author, and PublishAmerica then backed out.

prompt: Naked Came the Stranger was credited to an invented author, Penelope __________.
explanation: McGrady's sister-in-law posed as Penelope Ashe for the book jacket and interviews. The real authors were reporters at Newsday.

prompt: Why was Max Harris taken to court in 1944 after publishing the Ern Malley poems?
options: The police said the poems were indecent
He was charged with fraud for inventing Ern Malley
McAuley and Stewart sued him for using their poems
He broke wartime rules on printing paper
correctAnswer: The police said the poems were indecent
explanation: South Australian police charged him under the Indecent Advertisements Act, and he was fined £5. The detective admitted he did not know what one of the offending words meant.

prompt: Match each name to its part in a literary hoax:

pairs.right: A dead young poet who never existed
The editor who published the fake poems
The invented author of Naked Came the Stranger
The Atlanta Nights byline, a pun on travesty

explanation: Three of these four never existed: only Max Harris was real, and he was the one fooled. Penelope Ashe fronted a best-seller that sold even better once the joke came out.

prompt: Why should Romain Gary not have been able to win the Prix Goncourt in 1975?
options: He had already won it in 1956, and it goes to an author only once
He was not a French citizen
He sat on the Goncourt jury
The prize is only for first novels
correctAnswer: He had already won it in 1956, and it goes to an author only once
explanation: He won the second time as Émile Ajar, with his cousin's son Paul Pavlowitch playing Ajar in public. Pavlowitch revealed the truth in a memoir in 1981, the year after Gary's death.

prompt: The person who appeared in public as JT LeRoy, in a wig and sunglasses, was Laura Albert herself.
explanation: Albert wrote the books, but the public JT LeRoy was Savannah Knoop, the half-sibling of Albert's partner Geoffrey Knoop. Knoop later told the story in a memoir, Girl Boy Girl: How I Became JT LeRoy.

prompt: Helen Darville published The Hand That Signed the Paper under the invented name Helen __________.
explanation: The invented Ukrainian background helped persuade the Vogel judges that the book was authentic. After the August 1995 revelations it was reissued under the name Helen Darville.

prompt: In 2007 a Manhattan jury ruled against Laura Albert in a suit brought by a film company. What had she done?
options: Signed a film option contract for Sarah using the name JT LeRoy
Copied passages from another writer's novel
Sold the same film rights to two companies
Failed to deliver a screenplay she had been paid for
correctAnswer: Signed a film option contract for Sarah using the name JT LeRoy
explanation: The jury found fraud and breach of contract and awarded Antidote International Films $116,500. A judge later ordered Albert to pay about $350,000 more in legal fees and costs.

prompt: Match each name to its part in these stories:

pairs.right: Pen name that won Romain Gary a second Goncourt
Gary's cousin's son, who played Ajar in public
Appeared at readings as JT LeRoy
Invented Ukrainian identity behind a Miles Franklin winner

explanation: All three hoaxes turned on the gap between a book and the person readers believed had written it. Gary's and Albert's personas were played in public by stand-ins; Darville played hers herself.

prompt: How much of The Mystery of Edwin Drood had Dickens completed when he died?
options: Six of a planned twelve monthly installments
Everything except the final chapter
Only the opening chapter
Ten of a planned twelve installments
correctAnswer: Six of a planned twelve monthly installments
explanation: The surviving half sets up Edwin's disappearance and stops. Among Dickens's possible titles were "The Flight of Edwin Drood" and "Edwin Drood in Hiding", so even Edwin's death is uncertain.

prompt: At the 1914 mock trial of John Jasper, the jury, led by George Bernard Shaw, found him guilty of manslaughter.
explanation: Shaw admitted the verdict had been arranged over lunch as a compromise. Chesterton, as judge, then committed everyone in the room except himself for contempt of court.

prompt: The only part of the Codex Seraphinianus anyone has decoded is its page numbering, which is written mostly in base __________.
explanation: Ivan Derzhanski found twenty-one digits, from 0 to 20, plus quirky rules for bigger numbers. Serafini says the rest means nothing: he wanted the script to give readers the feeling children have in front of books they cannot yet understand.

prompt: What is the earliest printed source known to Quote Investigator that credits Hemingway with "For sale: baby shoes, never worn"?
options: A 1989 play about Hemingway
A letter Hemingway wrote in the 1920s
A 1906 newspaper classified ad
Hemingway's Nobel Prize speech
explanation: The 1906 ad was real, but it offered a baby carriage and had nothing to do with Hemingway. His name only became attached to the idea decades after his death in 1961.

prompt: Match each person to their part in these stories:

pairs.right: Judge at the 1914 trial of John Jasper
Wrote the Drood musical where the audience picks the killer
Suggested the story title "Little Shoes, Never Worn" in 1917

explanation: Holmes's audience-vote musical won the 1986 Tony Award for Best Musical. Kane's 1917 title is one of the clearest ancestors of the six-word story later pinned on Hemingway.
